item.title: Why Private Capital Can Smooth a Portfolio's Ride
item.summary: Private equity and private debt hold different companies, sectors and risk exposures than listed stocks and bonds, so adding them can lower a portfolio's overall risk. Part of the apparent benefit comes from infrequent, appraisal-style valuation, so a careful investor treats the reported figures with caution.

sections.heading: The core idea: different bets, not just more bets
sections.body_markdown: **Diversification** means combining assets whose returns do not move in lockstep, so that a bad stretch for one is partly offset by the others. The measure of 'moving in lockstep' is **correlation**, a number from $-1$ to $+1$. The lower the correlation between a new holding and your existing portfolio, the more it can reduce total risk. Think of a restaurant that serves both hot soup and ice cream: it earns something in any weather. **Private capital** (private equity and private debt) is a candidate for the ice cream stand, because it gives access to businesses that stock exchanges do not list.

sections.heading: Where the diversification comes from
sections.body_markdown: Private equity is ownership of companies that are not publicly traded. Private debt is lending to such companies outside the public bond market. Several features can make their returns behave differently from listed assets. (1) **Different borrowers and companies.** Private borrowers tend to be smaller and more focused, so their success depends more on how they compete within their industry than on the broad fortunes of the economy. (2) **Different sector mix.** Private credit often lends to firms owned by private equity sponsors, and those firms sit in industries weighted quite differently from public indexes. (3) **Concentrated, selective portfolios.** A private credit fund may hold only about 30–60 positions, which differs from a typical listed bond portfolio, and different managers' funds also overlap little with each other. (4) **Floating rates.** Private loans usually pay interest that resets with market rates, so they have very little **interest rate duration** (sensitivity of value to changes in interest rates). Rising rates therefore hurt them less than fixed-rate bonds. (5) **No sale needed at the end.** A private loan simply matures at par, so the market mood at exit matters less, unless the borrower defaults. Real estate debt illustrates the result: in one 20-year data set, commercial mortgage returns had roughly zero correlation with US and global equities (about $-0.02$ and $0.01$) but a high correlation (0.83) with non-agency CMBS, a related type of debt security. Diversification therefore depends on what you compare against.

sections.heading: The catch: smoothed numbers flatter the story
sections.body_markdown: Private assets are not priced every second. Their values come from **appraisals** (an expert's opinion) or from infrequent fund valuations. Appraisers tend to adjust slowly, partly through **anchoring**, which means leaning too heavily on earlier beliefs. The resulting series is **smoothed**: it moves less than a market price would. Smoothing lowers measured volatility and measured correlation with other assets, yet it barely changes the long-run average return. Reported risk is therefore too low, and the diversification benefit looks bigger than it really is. Managers can add to the distortion by choosing which holdings to re-value. Not all the low volatility is an illusion. Floating rates and the inability to panic-sell in a long-term fund structure are genuine reasons. The honest conclusion is that the benefit is real but probably smaller than the raw statistics suggest.

sections.heading: Putting numbers on it
sections.body_markdown: For a portfolio of two assets, the standard deviation depends on both asset risks and on their correlation. When correlation equals 1, portfolio risk is just the weighted average of the two standard deviations, so there is no benefit. Any correlation below 1 pulls portfolio risk below that average. This is why a lower measured correlation matters, and why understated correlation from smoothing overstates the benefit. Spreading private commitments over several years (**vintages**) and several managers adds a further layer of diversification inside the private allocation.

worked_example.problem: A portfolio holds 70% public equities (standard deviation 18%) and 30% in a private credit fund (reported standard deviation 8%). The reported correlation between the two is 0.20. Compute the portfolio standard deviation as a percentage to two decimals, and compare it with the weighted average of the two standard deviations.
steps: Covariance term, $2 w_1 w_2 \sigma_1 \sigma_2 \rho = 2 \times 0.7 \times 0.3 \times 0.18 \times 0.08 \times 0.2 = 0.0012096$. Keystrokes: 2 × .7 × .3 × .18 × .08 × .2 = then STO 3.
Add the three pieces to get the portfolio variance. Keystrokes: RCL 1 + RCL 2 + RCL 3 = gives 0.0176616.
Take the square root with the √x function to get 0.1329, which is 13.29%.

Compare: the weighted average of the standard deviations is $0.7 \times 18\% + 0.3 \times 8\% = 15.00\%$ (the result if correlation were 1). The low correlation lowers risk by about 1.7 percentage points. If smoothing has understated the correlation or the fund's risk, the true benefit is smaller.
worked_example.answer: The portfolio standard deviation is 13.29%, versus 15.00% if correlation were 1.

formulas.name: Two-asset portfolio standard deviation
formulas.where: $\sigma_p$ = portfolio standard deviation; $w_1,w_2$ = portfolio weights (summing to 1); $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ = standard deviations of the two assets; $\rho_{12}$ = correlation between the two assets' returns.

exam_traps: Treating a low reported correlation or volatility for private assets as fully reliable. Appraisal smoothing biases both downward, which overstates the diversification benefit.
Believing smoothing also lowers long-run average returns. It mainly affects measured volatility and correlation, and has minimal effect on average return.

Assuming private credit is low risk because its volatility looks low. Part of the low volatility is optical (no daily marking to market), even though floating rates and long fund lock-ups add real stability.
Forgetting that diversification is relative. Real estate debt had about zero correlation with equities but a high correlation (0.83) with non-agency CMBS.
Computing portfolio risk as the weighted average of the standard deviations. That is correct only when correlation is 1, and it hides the diversification benefit.

item.stem: Which statement best describes a source of diversification that private credit offers relative to a portfolio of listed bonds?

options.text: It lends to large mature issuers whose results track the broad listed market closely.
options.explanation: Wrong: this reverses the facts. Private borrowers are usually smaller, narrower businesses, so their results depend more on competing within their industry than on the broad market.

options.text: It lends to smaller, focused firms and gives a different sector mix from listed indexes.
options.explanation: Correct: borrowers differ from the constituents of listed portfolios and sector exposure differs, partly because many are owned by private equity sponsors, so overlap is low.

options.text: It holds far more positions than a typical listed bond portfolio, spreading risk widely.
options.explanation: Wrong: this confuses breadth with diversification. Alternative credit funds are usually concentrated, with roughly 30–60 positions.

item.stem: A portfolio is 50% public equity and 50% a private equity fund. Each has an annual standard deviation of 20%, and the correlation between their returns is 0.5. What is the portfolio standard deviation? Round to two decimals in percent.

options.explanation: Wrong: this drops the covariance term, which is the same as assuming a correlation of zero. The correlation here is 0.5, not 0.
Wrong: this takes the weighted average of the standard deviations, which is valid only if correlation is 1.

item.stem: An investor allocates to private real assets whose value is based on appraisals. What is the most likely effect of appraisal smoothing on the investor's analysis?

options.text: Reported volatility and correlation look lower than reality, so the diversification benefit is overstated.
options.explanation: Correct: slow-moving appraisals mute reported changes in value, which understates risk and correlation while leaving average returns largely intact.

options.text: Reported long-run average returns are cut sharply, so the diversification benefit is understated.
options.explanation: Wrong: smoothing has minimal impact on long-term average returns. It mainly affects measured volatility and correlation.

options.text: Reported volatility looks higher than reality, so the investor overestimates the risk of the asset.
options.explanation: Wrong direction: smoothing mutes price changes, so risk is underestimated rather than overestimated.

item.stem: A portfolio is 75% public equity (standard deviation 16%) and 25% a private fund whose reported standard deviation is 9%. The reported correlation between them is 0.10. Using these reported figures, what is the portfolio standard deviation? Round to two decimals in percent.

options.explanation: Wrong: this is the weighted average of 16% and 9%, which ignores the correlation (it assumes a correlation of 1).
Wrong: this is the variance (0.0154) presented as a percentage. The final step of taking the square root was skipped.

item.stem: A private credit fund reports much lower volatility and a lower correlation with equities than a listed high-yield bond index. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: The difference is entirely genuine, because private borrowers are always safer than public issuers.
options.explanation: Wrong: this ignores the optical effect of infrequent valuation and the fact that private borrowers are not inherently safer.

options.text: The difference is entirely an accounting artifact, because fundamentals play no role in it.
options.explanation: Wrong: fundamentals matter. Floating-rate loans have little interest rate duration, and long-term fund structures prevent panic selling.

options.text: Part is genuine (floating rates, no forced selling) and part is optical, so the benefit is somewhat overstated.
options.explanation: Correct: real drivers coexist with the reduced-volatility appearance caused by not marking to market daily and having no outside price reference.

item.stem: In a 20-year data set, a commercial real estate private debt index had a correlation of −0.02 with US equities and 0.83 with non-agency CMBS. Which conclusion is most reasonable?

options.text: The −0.02 shows it reliably rises when US equities fall, so it works as a hedge.
options.explanation: Wrong: −0.02 is essentially zero correlation, not a strong negative relationship. It indicates little linear link, not an offsetting move.

options.text: It diversified US equities well but offered little diversification relative to non-agency CMBS.
options.explanation: Correct: near-zero correlation with equities gives strong diversification, while a correlation of 0.83 means it moves closely with CMBS.

options.text: The 0.83 shows it diversifies non-agency CMBS especially well, since the figure is large.
options.explanation: Wrong: this confuses a high correlation with a good diversifier. Diversification improves as correlation falls.

item.stem: An analyst adjusts for appraisal smoothing. A portfolio is 75% public equity (standard deviation 16%) and 25% a private asset. Unsmoothed estimates give the private asset a standard deviation of 18% and a correlation of 0.40 with public equity. What is the portfolio standard deviation? Round to two decimals in percent.

options.explanation: Wrong: this reuses the smoothed inputs (9% standard deviation, 0.10 correlation) instead of the unsmoothed estimates, so it still shows the overstated diversification benefit.
Wrong: this omits the covariance term (0.0144 + 0.002025, then the square root), which ignores the 0.40 correlation.

item.stem: A fund investor currently commits all private equity capital to a single vintage year. What is the diversification benefit of spreading commitments across several vintage years?

options.text: It removes the illiquidity of the underlying private fund investments.
options.explanation: Wrong: vintage diversification does not change the long lock-up or illiquidity of each fund.

options.text: It guarantees the portfolio's correlation with public equity falls to zero.
options.explanation: Wrong: spreading commitments does not guarantee any particular correlation, and the underlying companies remain exposed to economic conditions.

options.text: It reduces dependence on market conditions at one entry point, which affects prices paid and exits.
options.explanation: Correct: investing in only one year ties results to the conditions of that period, so spreading commitments lowers that concentration.

item.front: Why can private credit diversify a portfolio of listed bonds?
item.back: Borrowers are smaller and more focused, the sector mix differs from listed indexes, portfolios are concentrated, and loans are floating-rate with little interest rate duration.

item.front: What does appraisal smoothing do to reported volatility, correlation and average return?
item.back: It lowers reported volatility and correlation, so risk is understated and diversification overstated. It has minimal impact on long-run average return.

item.front: When does a two-asset portfolio standard deviation equal the weighted average of the two standard deviations?
item.back: Only when the correlation between the assets is +1. Any lower correlation gives a portfolio standard deviation below that average.

item.front: Is the low reported volatility of private credit entirely an illusion?
item.back: No. Part is optical (no daily marking to market), but part is real: floating rates mean little duration, and long-term structures prevent panic selling.
